explanations.answer: In a village on the plain of Ono
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Sanballat and Geshem say, "Come, let us meet together in one of the villages on the plain of Ono." (Nehemiah 6:2) Sanballat and Geshem are two of the enemies who've been pestering Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. A village meeting sounds friendly, but the text says they were planning to harm him.

explanations.answer: In the royal palace at Susa
explanations.explanation: Susa is the royal city in the story of Nehemiah's start, so I see why it came to mind. But Sanballat and Geshem name a village on the plain of Ono (Nehemiah 6:2). Sanballat and Geshem are two enemies of Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. Nobody is inviting him to a palace here, and I think a fancy address would have made the invite look even better.

Samaria is a real place, but it's not the one on this invite. Sanballat and Geshem ask Nehemiah to meet in one of the villages on the plain of Ono (Nehemiah 6:2). Sanballat and Geshem are two of the enemies working against Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. The text says they were planning to harm him, so the address was the least of the problems.

I'd have loved for that to be true, friend, but the text says otherwise. Right after the invite, it says, "But they were planning to harm me." (Nehemiah 6:2) Sanballat and Geshem, two of Nehemiah's enemies, were smiling on the outside and scheming on the inside. A friendly meeting on the plain of Ono was never friendly.

Right, baker. Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, says it plainly: "But they were planning to harm me." (Nehemiah 6:2) Sanballat and Geshem, two of his enemies, sent a nice invite with a not-nice plan behind it. That's like a free cookie coupon that turns out to be a sales pitch, only a lot more serious.

explanations.answer: He's doing a great work and can't stop
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Nehemiah answers, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?" (Nehemiah 6:3) He's talking to Sanballat and Geshem, two enemies who want him off the wall. He doesn't argue or explain his whole life. He just says no and goes back to work.

explanations.answer: He's too sick to make the long trip
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Nehemiah was sick. His answer is, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down." (Nehemiah 6:3) The reason is the work itself. Sanballat and Geshem, two of his enemies, wanted him to leave it, and he wouldn't. I think a sick note would have given them a new excuse to keep inviting him.

explanations.answer: He's waiting for orders from the king
explanations.explanation: Good guess if you remember the king in this story, but Nehemiah never says that. He sends back, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down." (Nehemiah 6:3) Sanballat and Geshem, two of his enemies, got a reason about the work and nothing else. He asks them, "Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?"

That's right, baker. The text says, "Four times they sent me the same message, and each time I gave the same reply." (Nehemiah 6:4) Nehemiah doesn't get louder or fancier. He just repeats himself, four times in a row. I've told myself "just one more cookie" more often than that, and my answers were never identical.

I get it, you'd think four invites would wear him down. But the text says, "each time I gave the same reply." (Nehemiah 6:4) Nehemiah never turns up the heat or loses his cool. His answer stays steady while the invites keep coming from his enemies. Same answer, every time.

Not longer, friend. Nehemiah says it outright: "each time I gave the same reply." (Nehemiah 6:4) Same reply means the same words, so there was nothing added to stretch it out. I think after the first answer he already had it ready to go.

Look again, baker. The text says the servant had "an unsealed letter" in his hand (Nehemiah 6:5). Unsealed means open, so anybody could read it along the way. The writer doesn't say why it was left open, so I won't guess, but it's a detail worth noticing.

Right, baker. Sanballat's young servant had "an unsealed letter" in his hand (Nehemiah 6:5). Unsealed means it wasn't closed up, so it could be read by anyone. The text doesn't tell us why, so I'll just say it's a detail the writer wanted us to catch.

Yes, baker. The letter says, "It is reported among the nations—and Geshem agrees—that you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall." (Nehemiah 6:6) Nehemiah later answers, "There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) So the revolt story was Sanballat's idea, not the truth.

That's a believable reason to build a wall, but it's not what the letter says. It says the Jews are "plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall." (Nehemiah 6:6) Sanballat is accusing them of rebelling, not hiding. Nehemiah calls the whole thing an invention (Nehemiah 6:8).

Taxes never come up in this letter. The charge is that Nehemiah and the Jews are "plotting to revolt, and this is why you are building the wall." (Nehemiah 6:6) That's a much scarier accusation than a toll booth. Nehemiah answers that Sanballat is inventing it in his own mind (Nehemiah 6:8).

That's the one, baker. The letter says, "According to these reports, you are to become their king." (Nehemiah 6:6) It's a charge made to sound serious, and Nehemiah calls it an invention (Nehemiah 6:8). The word is in the letter, but nothing says it came from Nehemiah.

Close in sound, maybe, but the letter doesn't say priest. It says, "you are to become their king." (Nehemiah 6:6) A king is the worry, because a king means a revolt, and a revolt is the kind of rumor Sanballat wanted spreading. Nehemiah says Sanballat made it up (Nehemiah 6:8).

Prophets do show up in this letter, but not as the title. The letter says Nehemiah is "to become their king," and that he appointed prophets to announce it (Nehemiah 6:6-7). So the prophets are part of the accusation, not the job he's accused of taking. It's a story with a lot of moving parts, and none of them true.

Yes, baker. Nehemiah writes back, "There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) He doesn't go looking for who started it. He tells Sanballat, the enemy who sent the letter, that he made it up himself. Short, calm and no meeting required.

The letter does mention the king, warning that the rumors will reach him (Nehemiah 6:7). But Nehemiah doesn't blame the court. He says, "you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) Sanballat is the one he's pointing at.

Ono is where Sanballat and Geshem wanted to meet (Nehemiah 6:2), not where the rumors came from. Nehemiah answers Sanballat, "There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) So the blame lands on Sanballat, not on a village. I think the villages are relieved.

That's right, baker. Nehemiah says, "For they were all trying to frighten us, saying, 'Their hands will be weakened in the work, and it will never be finished.'" (Nehemiah 6:9) The letters and invites weren't just talk. Nehemiah says they were meant to scare the Jews off the work.

It's true, friend. Nehemiah says, "For they were all trying to frighten us, saying, 'Their hands will be weakened in the work, and it will never be finished.'" (Nehemiah 6:9) The enemies wanted the Jews scared and the work stalled. All those messages had a purpose.

Yes, baker. Right after naming what the enemies were saying, Nehemiah prays, "But now, my God, strengthen my hands." (Nehemiah 6:9) The enemies said the Jews' hands would be weakened, so he asks God for the opposite. It's a short prayer, and I love that it's right in the middle of the story.

It's an understandable thing to ask, but that isn't his prayer. Nehemiah says, "But now, my God, strengthen my hands." (Nehemiah 6:9) He asks for strength for the work, not quiet from his enemies. I think that's a good prayer for a Monday.

More workers would be handy, but that isn't what he asks. He prays, "But now, my God, strengthen my hands." (Nehemiah 6:9) The enemies were saying the work would never be finished, so his prayer answers that. It's about his own hands, not the crew size.

That's right, baker. Shemaiah, a man confined to his house, says, "Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors." (Nehemiah 6:10) His warning is that they're coming to kill Nehemiah by night. Notice he's asking Nehemiah to go inside and lock up.

A palace would sound safe, but Shemaiah doesn't name one. He says, "Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors." (Nehemiah 6:10) Shemaiah is the man confined to his house who gave this warning. It's the temple he points to, with the doors shut behind them.

A tower is good for lookouts, but it's not in this verse. Shemaiah says, "Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors." (Nehemiah 6:10) He's the man confined to his house who warned Nehemiah about a plot. The plan was to hide inside the temple.

Not quite, friend. Nehemiah answers, "Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!" (Nehemiah 6:11) He turns Shemaiah down flat. No hiding, no running, and no locking up the doors.

Right, baker. Nehemiah says, "Should a man like me run away? Should one like me go into the temple to save his own life? I will not go!" (Nehemiah 6:11) He says no to Shemaiah, a man confined to his house who had warned him of a plot. He asks two questions and gives one answer. I'd have taken a lot longer to say that, and I'd have asked to think about it.

That's right, baker. Nehemiah says he realized God had not sent Shemaiah, but "that he had uttered this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him." (Nehemiah 6:12) So the warning sounded holy but was paid for. Tobiah and Sanballat were the same enemies behind the earlier letters.

The priests aren't mentioned here at all. Nehemiah says Shemaiah gave the prophecy "because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him." (Nehemiah 6:12) Tobiah and Sanballat were two of his enemies from earlier in the chapter. The hiring was the whole reason.

That would make Shemaiah an honest mistake, but the text says something else. Nehemiah says Shemaiah gave the prophecy "because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him." (Nehemiah 6:12) It was a paid job from his enemies, not a rumor he picked up. Nehemiah also realized God had not sent him.

explanations.answer: He would sin and get a bad name
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Nehemiah says Shemaiah was hired "to intimidate me so that I would sin by doing as he suggested, so they could give me a bad name in order to discredit me." (Nehemiah 6:13) The plan wasn't just to scare him. It was to get him to do something wrong so they could spoil his name.

explanations.answer: He would be trapped and arrested
explanations.explanation: Being trapped sounds like a good guess, but the text doesn't say arrest. Nehemiah says the aim was "so that I would sin by doing as he suggested, so they could give me a bad name in order to discredit me." (Nehemiah 6:13) The goal was a spoiled reputation. The enemies wanted him to sin first.

explanations.answer: He would give away the city's plans
explanations.explanation: Nothing about city plans shows up in the text. Nehemiah says Shemaiah was hired "to intimidate me so that I would sin by doing as he suggested, so they could give me a bad name in order to discredit me." (Nehemiah 6:13) The target was Nehemiah's name, not any secrets.

Yes, baker. The text says, "So the wall was completed in fifty-two days." (Nehemiah 6:15) That's a little over seven weeks, and all of it with enemies sending invites and letters. I can't promise a batch of cookies in that kind of weather.

Ninety is a nice round number, but the text gives a shorter one. It says, "the wall was completed in fifty-two days." (Nehemiah 6:15) Fifty-two days, with all that opposition. Round numbers are for people who didn't have this much to push through.

Forty comes up a lot in the Bible, so I see why it popped in. But this verse says, "the wall was completed in fifty-two days." (Nehemiah 6:15) Fifty-two, not forty. Twelve more days, and every one of them counted.

That's right, baker. The text says, "all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened." (Nehemiah 6:16) These were the enemies who had been trying to scare the Jews. Now the fear was on their side.

Joy would be a strange reaction for people who had been working against the wall. The text says, "all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened." (Nehemiah 6:16) They'd been trying to frighten the Jews, and now the finished wall left them afraid instead.

Proud doesn't fit the mood of these nations. The text says, "all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened." (Nehemiah 6:16) Afraid and disheartened, not proud. I think the finished wall wasn't what they were hoping to hear about.

Yes, baker. The text says the nations were afraid and disheartened "for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God." (Nehemiah 6:16) The text says they realized it was God's work, and that's why they were shaken. The wall was finished, and they knew whose hand was in it.

No army is mentioned in this verse. The text says the nations were afraid and disheartened "for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God." (Nehemiah 6:16) Their fear came from seeing God's hand in the work. It wasn't about soldiers.

explanations.answer: They hear the king approves it
explanations.explanation: The king isn't part of the reason in this verse. The text says they were afraid and disheartened "for they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God." (Nehemiah 6:16) They saw God behind the work. That's what shook them.

Yes, baker. The text says, "For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, since he was a son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah." (Nehemiah 6:18) Tobiah was one of Nehemiah's enemies, and yet he had ties inside Judah. The text gives the oath and the family link as the reason.

It's true, friend. The text says, "For many in Judah were bound by oath to him." (Nehemiah 6:18) Tobiah, one of Nehemiah's enemies, had ties with plenty of people in Judah. His marriage into Shecaniah's family is the reason the verse gives.

That's right, baker. The text says, "these nobles kept reporting to me Tobiah's good deeds, and they relayed my words to him." (Nehemiah 6:19) Tobiah, the enemy from earlier in the chapter, had friends in high places. The nobles went back and forth between the two sides.

It's true, friend. The text says, "these nobles kept reporting to me Tobiah's good deeds, and they relayed my words to him." (Nehemiah 6:19) So the nobles of Judah were praising Tobiah to Nehemiah, the same Tobiah who had been working against him. They were carrying words both ways.

Yes, baker. The verse ends, "And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me." (Nehemiah 6:19) The nobles were praising Tobiah to Nehemiah, but Tobiah's own letters were meant to scare him. The story isn't done yet, so keep your oven mitts on.

Winning him over would be a nice twist, but that isn't the purpose. The verse says, "And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me." (Nehemiah 6:19) Tobiah wanted Nehemiah scared, not charmed. The nobles may have praised Tobiah, but his letters tell the real story.

Peace would have been a welcome change, but the verse says otherwise. "And Tobiah sent letters to intimidate me." (Nehemiah 6:19) Tobiah's letters were meant to scare Nehemiah, not make peace. I think Nehemiah's mailbox needed a break.
